Model, agent, and catalog discovery uses runtime.snapshot.get. Skills use the session-aware skills.list and skills.get methods because visibility depends on the governing run policy and session overlay. session.list returns root sessions only: a delegated child is selected as part of its root's tree, not as a top-level entry, and stays reachable via session.tree, session.children, session.get, and session.resume.

docs.title: Runtimes
docs.text:
A session uses the tools and workspace context of the runtimes it is attached to. A RuntimeAttachment is { name, runtime_id, kind, workspace? }: the session-unique attachment name (also the tool prefix on name collisions), the template's runtime_id, the runtime's kind (global or coding), and the canonical workspace the runtime reported, if any. The session create, get, and resume results carry the session's attachments in attach order; clients follow later changes through the runtime_attached and runtime_detached events of the session.

session.create attaches global unless global is false, then each entry of runtimes in order; without runtimes it attaches local, the coding runtime for the daemon's working directory. An empty runtimes list creates a session with no coding runtime. Instances that are not running are started first, and a failure creates no session.

session.runtime.attach and session.runtime.detach are rejected while the session has an active run (session running). Attach starts the instance when needed and records nothing when that fails. The attachment's name is the name the instance reports (global, or <runtime ID>_<workspace basename> for a coding runtime), suffixed _2, _3, ... when the session already has an attachment of that name; attaching an instance a session already has is an error. A template whose definition takes a workspace requires workspace; for any other template, including global and local, supplying one is an error. Attaching a runtime ID without a template is an unknown runtime error. Besides global and local, the templates are the configured [runtimes.<id>] tables. The daemon passes workspace to the runtime exactly as given; the attachment records the canonical path the runtime reported, and two spellings of one workspace share an instance.

runtimes.list returns each template's runtime_id and whether it takes_workspace, and each instance's runtime_id, reported attachment_name, kind, workspace, and platform once started, its status (starting, ready, reconnecting, failed, or stopped), and a failure message.

runtimes.reconnect retries an instance now: a failed instance is started again, under a new generation, and keeps its identity; an instance that is not running is started; a ready or reconnecting one is left as it is. workspace follows the attach rule, and for a failed instance it is the workspace that runtimes.list reports. A start that fails is an error with the reason, and is also reported in runtimes.changed. Retrying global also retries its failed MCP servers.

docs.title: Model availability
docs.text:
Protocol 24 (runtime snapshot schema 6) makes unusable models visible instead of silently dropping them. snapshot.models still lists only selectable models. Each ProviderDescriptor additionally carries:

  • model_counts: available, quarantined, unsupported, needs_setup, and needs_credentials counts over the provider's catalog rows (deprecated, disabled, and non-text models are not counted).
  • unavailable_models: one entry per unusable model with id, display_name, kind (the four unavailable kinds above), and a nullable reason (the quarantine code or compiler reason). The list is strictly sorted by id and is populated only for configured (authored or stored) providers; unconfigured providers report counts alone.
  • documentation_url and environment: the models.dev doc URL and env variable names. They are display hints; cookie never reads those variables.

catalog_state.age is current, older_than_seven_days, or older_than_thirty_days for the selected catalog body, alongside the existing stale flag, quarantine counts, and nullable last_error.

docs.title: Goal/producer integration handoff
docs.text:
The engine implements these methods through its per-session actor. Goal mutations are root-only; producer inspection is available for any owned session. Goal/producer request shapes remain unchanged. Session protocol 18 added declared tool-output channels, terminal output references, and independent UI display. Plugin extension 0.0.6 uses typed terminal single/named output and final display; package versions are unchanged.

Surface Public contract Implementation owner Goal projection GoalState, GoalItem, GoalStatus, GoalId Engine; TUI renders durable events Goal read SessionGoalGetParams/Result, get_session_goal Engine; TUI/clients call async API Activation SessionGoalSetParams/Result, set_session_goal User-only root command, rejects active/paused goal Lifecycle SessionGoalLifecycleParams/Result, change_session_goal_lifecycle, GoalLifecycleAction User-only root pause/resume/cancel; reject stale/terminal goal Model tools GoalGetParams/Result, GoalUpdateParams/Result Root-only goal_get/goal_update, frozen at run admission Runtime inspection SessionProducersParams/Result, session_producers, ProducerRegistration, PluginRecoveryState Session runtime snapshot, not global catalog snapshot or persistence Plugin messaging ExtensionProducer{Register,Send,Discard,Unregister}Params/Result Engine request handlers; SDK mirrors register/send/discard/unregister Recovery handshake ExtensionRecoveryStartParams, ExtensionRecoveryCompleteParams/Result, ExtensionRecoveryOutcome plugin/recovery/start engine notification (no deadline/response); plugin completion request

Goal activation accepts an optional selection: RunSelection, including agent, model, variant, and preset. The engine validates and persists this selection before scheduling a wake, so it survives waiting for producers and restarting. Lifecycle requests accept selection only with action: "resume"; pause and cancel reject a supplied selection. Resuming without it preserves the goal's previous selection. If activation omitted it and no later resume supplied one, automatic runs use the latest persisted run selection, falling back to the session's creation selection. None of these changes mutate an already-running turn's frozen selection or attribution.

GoalItem { description, finished } has no item ID. GoalUpdateParams { items } replaces the entire ordered checklist through the session actor: the last accepted update wins for the current/latest session goal at actor acceptance. Model updates have no goal_id, expected_revision, or lost-update protection. An older run's update can intentionally affect a newly activated active or paused goal; updates reject if the current goal is absent or terminal. Internal GoalId and engine-owned GoalState.revision remain for durable state and reminder identity. User lifecycle RPC controls retain SessionGoalLifecycleParams.goal_id and expected_revision and reject stale identities and revisions; no model tool can set an objective or issue lifecycle commands. Empty lists preserve the active/paused lifecycle and can bootstrap an active goal without completion. The engine decides existing tool permission mapping: goal_get uses read, and goal_update uses write, both with resource goal:current. Ordinary permission rules still apply. There is no new permission action or goal configuration.

To preserve strictly increasing event revisions, an all-finished update appends checklist revision r+1, then completion revision r+2, and returns the final state. Recovery repairs a missing completion event after a committed all-finished checklist. Empty checklists never complete through this rule.

See Events for admission/commit coverage and owned-message discard, and Plugins for method names, idempotency, recovery, and the no-implicit-registration requirement.

docs.title: User steering
docs.text:
run.steer requires an active target run. It immediately appends user_input_admitted and returns { "accepted": true }; admission does not change model history. At each completed tool batch and no-tool completion boundary, all pending inputs are promoted FIFO as separate user_input_submitted events before the next request. A no-tool boundary with no pending input completes the run.

run.steer also returns the admission's user_input_seq. Terminal run events void anything still pending.

docs.title: The session's model selection
docs.text: A session has one model selection (agent, model, variant, preset) that every client shares. session.select_model validates a selection as a run start would and appends a runless session_model_selected event under the caller's origin; selecting what the session already has records nothing and returns { "changed": false }. cookie_agent_protocol::SessionModelState folds the session's selection from its events: the creation selection, then each run's selection and successful fallback, with an explicit pick replacing it and dropping any fallback the session had settled on. A run started without a selection (session.submit_input with selection omitted, or a queued input queued that way) uses it, and clients keep their drafts at it, so the latest pick from any client is what the next message runs on. A request that names its own selection still runs on that one.

docs.title: Submitting from several clients
docs.text:
session.submit_input is how clients send a message without first finding out whether the session is running. On the session's actor it either starts a run ({ "outcome": "started", "run_id" }), or, while a run is active, follows delivery:

  • steer admits the input as run.steer does: { "outcome": "steered", "run_id", "user_input_seq" }.
  • queue appends a runless user_input_queued event holding the input, its selection, and client_run_id: { "outcome": "queued", "queued_seq" }.

A run that starts or ends while the request is in flight only changes which outcome happens; the daemon retries a few times before answering with a session_running conflict. An omitted selection means the session's current selection. A plugin that handles the input yields { "outcome": "handled", "reason" }. Retrying the same client_run_id with the same input returns the original run or queue entry; different input is an idempotency_conflict.

When a run completes normally, the daemon starts a run with the oldest queued input under the origin of the client that queued it; that run's run_started carries the entry's client_run_id, which removes it from the queue. A failed, cancelled, or interrupted run voids every queued input, and the daemon appends user_input_queue_voided when a queued input cannot start at all. Clients reduce the queue with cookie_agent_protocol::QueuedInputs, as the daemon does.

session.recall_input takes back one pending steered input or one queued input by its seq. Only the client whose origin admitted it may do so: another client gets { "outcome": "not_owner" }. A pending input is withdrawn with user_input_recalled_v2 and a queued one with user_input_queue_recalled; both return { "outcome": "recalled", "input" }. An input that was already promoted, started, or voided returns { "outcome": "gone" }.

run.start on a session whose run is active fails with code -32602 and RunStartConflict data whose code is session_running, so a client can fall back to session.submit_input.

docs.title: Revert and fork
docs.text:
session.revert is idle-only. The target must be a positive existing sequence, and expected_last_seq must be the session's current last event sequence: a session that has moved on since the client looked (another client's turn, say) is refused with code -32602, message stale revert, and SessionRevertConflict data carrying current_last_seq, so a revert never deletes what the requester has not seen. The engine removes every event after it from the log (a run left with nothing but its run_started goes too), closes any run, tool call, internal agent, or approval the cut left open, and deletes the subagent sessions created by removed delegations; a running one refuses the revert. Later appends reuse the freed sequence numbers. Subscribers receive a rewound notification (see Subscriptions). Logs from before protocol 28 may still hold session_reverted markers, which readers apply as before: each hides what followed its target on the branch visible when it was written.

session.fork takes a client_fork_id: while the daemon runs, a retry with the same key and target returns the first fork instead of making another, and the same key with a different target is an idempotency_conflict. session.fork may read an active source but requires a persisted prefix that contains a submitted user message. The fork copies that prefix exactly under a new session ID, closes any copied in-flight run locally, appends (fork) to the title, and continues with new physical sequences.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: Notification Payload runtime.changed Previous revision, complete snapshot, sorted change reasons events.subscription One stored event, live-only stream output, a session sequence gap, or a rewind events.plugin Session-scoped non-durable plugin event sessions.changed One session index change: upserted, removed, approvals_changed, permission_mode_changed, or resync mcp.changed MCP server configuration or status changed; optional failures runtimes.changed A runtime template was registered or an instance's status changed; optional failures

docs.title: Daemon-wide changes
docs.text:
runtime.changed, sessions.changed, mcp.changed, and runtimes.changed reach every connection from its handshake on, whether or not it subscribed to any session, so each client sharing a daemon stays current with what the others do. Clients ignore notification methods they do not know.

sessions.changed carries one change, tagged by change:

change Fields Sent when upserted session (SessionMeta) A session, root or delegated, is created, first persisted, or reverted, or its status or title changes removed session_id A revert deleted a delegated session approvals_changed root_session_id, session_id An approval in any session of the tree was requested, escalated, decided, or cancelled; approval.list for the root shows the result permission_mode_changed root_session_id, mode, changed_by session.set_permission_mode changed the tree's mode; changed_by is the caller's origin resync none This connection fell more than 256 changes behind and missed some; refetch session.list, approvals, and permission modes

The permission mode is runtime-only and has no event, so permission_mode_changed is the only way other clients learn of a change.

runtime.changed notifications form a chain through previous_revision. A connection that falls more than 64 notifications behind receives one with a null previous_revision, the current snapshot, and the reason resync; a client that holds a different revision refetches runtime.snapshot.get rather than trusting either. A status mcp.changed is an empty object; bursts coalesce into one notification, and a client refetches mcp.server.list. runtimes.changed works the same way for runtimes.list.

docs.title: Connection failures
docs.text:
When an MCP server fails to connect, or drops and does not reconnect, and when a runtime instance fails to start, the daemon sends one notification for it with a failures list to each connection subscribed (events.subscribe) to a session that uses it. Each entry names the affected session_ids among that connection's subscriptions:

Notification failures entry mcp.changed runtime_id hosting the server (global for top-level [mcp]), workspace of the hosting instance when its runtime has one, server, reason, session_ids runtimes.changed runtime_id, workspace when the template takes one, reason, session_ids

Subscribing to a session also sends the failures that already affect it, so a client that opens a session after its servers failed still learns why their tools are missing. Failures are live notifications, not session events; the TUI shows each as an error row in every named session it displays. failures is omitted when empty.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text:
mcp.server.list returns the servers of every runtime: the global runtime's top-level [mcp] servers first, then those each running coding runtime instance hosts from its template's mcp table. Each entry has the hosting runtime_id, the hosting instance's workspace (absent for global), name, source, definition, state, tool_count, message, and auth_in_progress. state is connected, connecting, reconnecting, failed, needs_auth, disabled, or disconnected. A reconnecting server dropped and is being restarted: its tools stay published and calls fail with the runtime_unavailable failure code until it reconnects or, after every attempt failed, becomes failed and its tools are dropped (see MCP). The mcp.server.* mutations and mcp.auth.* act on servers of the global runtime. mcp.server.reconnect { name, runtime_id?, workspace? } reconnects a server of any runtime and waits for the attempt: without runtime_id (or with global) a top-level server, otherwise the one the instance of runtime_id at workspace hosts, as mcp.server.list names them.

The shared client maps these to ClientDelivery variants (Live, replay deliveries, PluginEvent, RuntimeChanged, RecoveryFailed), so a UI consumes one ordered stream and never parses raw JSON-RPC frames.

Protocol 23 removed the events.tool_output_snapshot, events.tool_output_delta, and events.tool_output_gap notifications. Tool display comes from tool_call_progress and tool_call_terminated events; retained output is read through its artifact references.

Protocol 25 makes text_delta, reasoning_delta, and tool_call_progress live-only: events.subscription delivers them as transient messages carrying the durable after_seq they follow instead of a sequence of their own, and they are never stored or replayed. model_output_started durably marks where each streamed part began. See live-only stream output.

Protocol 27 moves the MCP OAuth callback to the client, so a daemon reached through a tunnel or on another machine can still be authorized from the client's browser. mcp.auth.begin requires redirect_uri, the client's own loopback callback (http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path> or http://[::1]:<port>/<path> with no query, fragment, or credentials). The client then sends the browser's redirect to the new mcp.auth.complete { server, callback_url }; the daemon keeps the PKCE verifier, exchanges the code, and stores the tokens, which never cross the connection. A callback_url that is not a redirect to the pending redirect_uri with a code or error parameter is rejected and leaves the flow waiting. Any other completion ends it. A begin with the pending redirect_uri returns the same authorization URL; one with a different redirect_uri replaces the pending flow. Protocol 26 shipped only in a nightly build and is not reused.

Protocol 30 lets a client configure permissions before a session exists. session.create accepts an optional permission_mode for the new tree and optional permission_rules, which are validated like any overlay (no duplicate action and pattern, at most 256) before the session is created and committed as its first session_permission_overlay_set event, so the first run already sees them. session.permission.preview { selection, rules } returns the effective permissions such a session would have, computed from the selection's frozen agent policy exactly as session.permission.get computes them for a live session.

Protocol 31 adds background jobs. ProducerOwner gains tool { tool_call_id } for the completion report of a job a tool call started (a bash call with background: true), and producer_message_accepted gains an optional retained_output naming the job's captured output artifacts. Older clients cannot decode the new owner variant, so the version moves.

Protocol 32 stops storing tool output that fits its preview anywhere but the result output. RetainedToolStream.reference and sha256 become optional and are absent for such a stream, and RetainedToolOutput.reference is absent when no stream needed an artifact. RetainedToolStream also gains dropped_bytes, present when output past the 128 MiB capture limit was not retained. Older clients require the now-optional fields, so the version moves.

Protocol 33 stops sending a tool result's display twice. When display occurs verbatim in output, PersistedToolResult carries display_span, the [start, end) byte range of output, in its place. Older clients reject the unknown field, so the version moves.

Session metadata includes additive skipped_events entries with the physical sequence (or source line number when no sequence was readable) and a safe reason. An empty array means the event log loaded without skipped records. Optional-field degradations remain available to the engine as load diagnostics but are not reported as skipped events.

See Events for event payloads and durability semantics.

docs.title: Runtime Protocol
docs.text:
The runtime protocol connects the daemon to a runtime: a source of tools and workspace context that runs outside the engine (see the runtimes specification). The daemon's built-in local coding runtime speaks it on a task of the daemon's own process over an in-memory frame pair; a configured [runtimes.<id>] template runs a command, typically ssh host cookie runtime coding --stdio --workspace {workspace}, and speaks it over the child's stdin and stdout. The local and remote paths are one code path. The global runtime does not speak it; the engine calls it in-process.

The wire types live in cookie_agent_runtime_api::protocol, the JSON-RPC peer both ends run in cookie_agent_runtime_api::rpc, the coding runtime's server in cookie_agent_coding_runtime::server, and the daemon's client in the engine's runtimes::remote module.

docs.title: Framing
docs.text:
• JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per frame: a frame of an in-memory transport, or one line of newline-delimited JSON over a byte stream such as a child's stdio (rpc::LineTransport).
  • Both ends send requests. The daemon drives tools; a runtime reports progress and background jobs back while a call runs. Request IDs are unsigned integers chosen by the sender.
  • Bounded. No frame exceeds 48 MiB (protocol::MAX_FRAME_BYTES), which fits an execute reply carrying the largest attachment as base64 next to a full tool result. A sender refuses to send a larger message; a receiver that gets one closes the connection.
  • Strict. Every message and every params or result object rejects unknown fields. A frame that is not a valid request, notification, or reply closes the connection. A request whose params do not match its method is answered with -32602, and the connection stays up.

docs.title: Version
docs.text: The protocol version is an integer, currently 1 (protocol::RUNTIME_PROTOCOL_VERSION). The daemon sends its version in runtime/initialize; a runtime that speaks another version fails the request with code -32010 and a message naming both versions, and the daemon checks the version in the reply the same way. There is no negotiation.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. The daemon connects (in-process: a new frame pair and a server task; a configured template: it runs the command in its own process group, a job object on Windows, with the daemon's environment plus the template's env) and sends runtime/initialize, all within the template's startup_timeout_ms. Every other request before it is answered with -32012; a second initialize with -32011. A child's stderr is kept as a bounded tail (the last 32 lines, at most 4 KiB) that failure reasons end with; nothing but protocol messages may appear on its stdout.
  2. Sessions use the instance: the daemon prepares, executes, and releases calls, and asks for AGENTS.md context at each root run's admission. A coding runtime reports its MCP servers' status as it changes (mcp/changed) and a changed tool list (runtime/tools_changed).
  3. The daemon sends runtime/shutdown when it shuts down, waits up to the template's shutdown_grace_ms for the answer, and closes the transport (a child's stdin); a child that has not exited after another grace is killed with its process group. The runtime answers, cancels every running call and background job, and stops. It also stops when its transport ends.

When the connection is lost while the instance is in use, every call in flight fails with runtime_unavailable and every running background job completes as failed (runtime … exited before the job finished). The instance becomes reconnecting: its tools stay published, calls fail fast with runtime_unavailable, and the daemon starts it again up to 3 times, after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s, sending runtime/initialize with the canonical workspace the instance reported. A restart that reports the same identity (runtime ID, kind, attachment name, workspace) revives the instance under a new generation: its tools are listed again, and a call published before the restart fails as operation_changed. When every attempt fails, the instance becomes failed, its tools leave the session's tool list, and clients are told the reason. A failed instance starts again when a session that uses it is created or opened, or on runtimes.reconnect. Calls are never retried transparently.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Direction Kind Purpose runtime/initialize daemon → runtime request Version, runtime ID, workspace, settings; returns identity, tools, skills runtime/tools_changed runtime → daemon notification The whole new tool list runtime/context daemon → runtime request AGENTS.md context for a run's preset runtime/shutdown daemon → runtime request Stop gracefully tool/prepare daemon → runtime request Prepare one turn's calls to this runtime tool/revalidate daemon → runtime request Check a prepared call can still run as approved tool/execute daemon → runtime request Run a prepared call; returns its terminal result tool/release daemon → runtime notification Discard a prepared call that will not run tool/progress runtime → daemon request Display and output deltas of an executing call tool/stdin daemon → runtime request Bytes for an interactive call's stdin tool/cancel daemon → runtime notification Cancel an executing call job/started runtime → daemon request An executing call reserves a background job job/progress runtime → daemon request Output of a background job job/completed runtime → daemon notification A background job finished with its report job/kill daemon → runtime notification Kill a background job mcp/changed runtime → daemon notification The status of the runtime's MCP servers, and the ones that failed mcp/reconnect daemon → runtime request Reconnect one MCP server, or retry every failed one

An unknown request is answered with -32601; an unknown notification is ignored.

docs.title: runtime/initialize
docs.text:
Params field Meaning version The daemon's protocol version. runtime_id The template's runtime ID, [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}. workspace The workspace path the daemon asks for, when the template has one, exactly as a session gave it: the runtime expands a leading ~ and resolves it on its own machine. Optional: a runtime started for one workspace (--workspace) uses its own, and refuses one that resolves elsewhere. settings.tool_output The [tool_output] preview limits: max_lines, max_bytes, head_lines, tail_lines. settings.agent_md max_bytes: files larger than this are skipped. At most the AGENTS.md event bound. settings.mcp_servers The template's MCP servers: name and config, the server's table as the [mcp.servers.<name>] schema reads it.

A runtime rejects settings its kind does not support with -32011, as it does a workspace it cannot open. MCP hosting is a feature of the coding kind: a runtime of another kind rejects a nonempty mcp_servers, and the daemon rejects an initialize reply whose kind hosts no MCP servers when it sent some (protocol::check_mcp_hosting). A coding runtime parses each server strictly and rejects the request when one does not parse or enables OAuth, which stays with the daemon's global runtime.

A coding runtime connects every enabled server before it answers: the reply comes once each server's first connection attempt and tool listing have finished, successfully or not, so the template's startup_timeout_ms must cover them. A server that fails publishes no tools; its status says why. The servers' tools join the declared tools as <server>_<tool>, with permission mcp, after the runtime's built-in tools, which keep their names: a server whose tool would take another tool's name fails, as in the global runtime. OAuth is never used: a remote server connects with its static headers only.

Result field Meaning version The runtime's protocol version. kind global or coding. attachment_name The name sessions attach the instance under: <runtime ID>_<workspace basename>, sanitized, for a coding runtime. workspace The canonical workspace on the runtime's machine. platform Operating system, as Rust's std::env::consts::OS names it. shell The shell bash runs. tools.tools Tool declarations: name, collision (prefix or fallback), permission (a permission action such as bash or read), description, parameters (JSON Schema), concurrency, result_truncation, output. tools.prompt_sections System prompt sections (title, body) the tools contribute. skills.skills Project skills: the SKILL.md text, source, absolute path and base_dir on the runtime's machine, and a sample of supporting_files. The daemon parses the text with the same rules as local discovery. skills.discoveries Every SKILL.md found, with precedence_winner. mcp_servers The status of each MCP server after its first connection attempt, in name order: name; state, one of connected, connecting, reconnecting, failed, disabled, or disconnected; message, why it failed; and tools, its tool names. Absent when the runtime hosts none.

docs.title: runtime/tools_changed
docs.text: Params are a new tools object as in the initialize result. The daemon uses it from the next model turn on.

docs.title: mcp/changed, mcp/reconnect
docs.text:
mcp/changed carries servers, the status of every MCP server the runtime hosts as in the initialize result, and failures, the servers that failed to connect or dropped and did not reconnect since the last report, each with server and reason. The runtime sends it after its initialize reply, whenever a status changes; a failure may arrive in a report of its own. The daemon shows the statuses in mcp.server.list and passes each failure to the clients viewing a session attached to the instance.

When a connected server drops, the runtime restarts it up to 3 times, after 1 s, 2 s, and 4 s. Meanwhile it is reconnecting, its tools stay declared, and calls fail with runtime_unavailable. A successful attempt restores the server with its current tool list; when every attempt fails, it becomes failed, a runtime/tools_changed drops its tools, and mcp/changed reports the failure.

mcp/reconnect params: server, optional. With a name, the runtime closes that server's connection and connects it again; without one, it retries every failed server. It answers {} once the attempts have finished, or {"error": …} for an unknown or disabled server or a failed attempt; the new status follows in mcp/changed. While one of the instance's servers is failed, the daemon sends it without a name when a session that uses the instance is created or opened, or when the instance is attached or retried, and the session's next run waits for the answer; it names a server for mcp.server.reconnect.

docs.title: runtime/context
docs.text: Params: preset, the run's agent preset (optional; must be a valid agent ID). Result: agent_md, the AGENTS.md entries in prompt order, and skipped, files over the size limit. The runtime applies the lookup to its workspace: the preset's .cookie-agent/agents/<preset>/AGENTS.md, else .cookie-agent/agents/AGENTS.md, then <workspace>/AGENTS.md. A file that exists but cannot be read fails the request with -32014 and data.path.

docs.title: tool/prepare
docs.text:
Params: session, run, turn (the agent, model, adapter, adapter family, and model capabilities of the turn), and calls (id, name, arguments; at most 256). The runtime prepares a turn's calls together, so calls on one target chain. The result has one entry per call, tagged by status:

  • prepared: prepared_id; operation, the prepared operation identity; policy_labels, one per operation resource; normalized_arguments; permission, the permission action; permission_resource, the resource of the normalized arguments; presentation, the call's title and display argument; and serialization_key, lowercase hex, when calls sharing it must run one at a time.
  • failed: error and the presentation to show for the failed call.

The runtime keeps a prepared call under its prepared_id until it is executed or released. Concurrency is declared per tool, not per call.

docs.title: tool/revalidate, tool/release
docs.text: Both take prepared_id. Revalidate answers {} or {"error": …}; release is a notification.

docs.title: tool/execute
docs.text:
Params field Meaning prepared_id The call to run; executing consumes it. session, run, turn As for prepare. stdin The daemon forwards stdin with tool/stdin. background The call may start background jobs.

The result's outcome is tagged by status: completed with the terminal output (single or streamed), the persisted result, and failed; or failed with an error. Next to it:

  • media: the bytes of every attachment the result references, as sha256 and base64 data, at most 25 MiB in all. The runtime gives each retained attachment the reference the daemon's content-addressed artifact store will give it; the daemon stores the bytes, checks each digest and reference, and rejects a result that references media it did not receive.
  • launched_jobs: the jobs the call reserved and launched. The daemon releases the others.

While a call runs, the runtime sends its progress with tool/progress (prepared_id, and progress: tool_call_id, message, display, and output chunks, under the 64 KiB and 8-stream delta bounds). It waits for each answer, so output reaches the daemon's capture in order, the daemon's capture limits reach the tool, and every chunk precedes the execute reply. The daemon owns capture, previews, and artifact retention.

tool/stdin carries prepared_id, base64 data (at most 1 MiB decoded), and eof. tool/cancel cancels the call; it still answers its execute request. The runtime registers an execution as the request arrives, so stdin and cancellation sent right after execute reach it.

docs.title: Background jobs
docs.text: A call that starts a background job (such as bash with background) reserves it with job/started (prepared_id, job); the daemon reserves its side, which owns the job's output capture and its completion message, and answers {} or an error. The job's output arrives with job/progress (job, progress), and its end with job/completed (job, report: summary, element, attributes, body). The daemon commits the completion as it does for an in-process job: only once the starting call is committed as completed. When the starting call never commits, is reverted, or its session is deleted, the daemon sends job/kill.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Code Meaning -32601 Unknown method. -32602 Params do not match the method. -32603 Internal error. -32010 Protocol version mismatch. -32011 The runtime rejects the initialize request or its settings. -32012 A request before runtime/initialize. -32013 Unknown prepared call or job. -32014 Reading the runtime's context failed; data.path names the file. -32015 The reply would exceed the frame bound.

Tool-level failures travel inside results as {"kind": …, "message": …}, where kind is the tool error kind (failed, operation_changed, resource_limit, permission_denied, timeout, runtime_unavailable, …).

docs.title: Schema Compatibility
docs.text:
Runtime configuration and agent documents are unversioned authored files parsed against the current shape. They reject schema and schema_version fields as hard errors rather than migrating or ignoring them. Session event history is also versionless and read best-effort. Versioned persisted and wire surfaces emit only their current version and reject unsupported versions.

Surface Current write Accepted reads Runtime configuration unversioned unversioned current shape Agent document unversioned unversioned current shape Protocol 19 19 Events and session JSONL versionless versionless plus legacy schema markers Session metadata unversioned unversioned current shape Runtime snapshot 5 5 Catalog cache 2 2 Provider store 3 3 Family recipe registry 1 1 In-memory model manifest (recorded run bindings) 1 1

Agent snapshots embedded in readable events upconvert supported historical shapes before validation. Delegation lifecycle records are ordinary parent session events; the removed delegations.jsonl surface and its schema versions are not read.

The protocol crate exports a JSON Schema set for the wire roots on demand through cargo run -p cookie_agent_protocol --example generate -- --output <directory>; no generated tree is checked in. crates/protocol/scripts/check-schema-additive.sh regenerates the schemas into a temporary directory and enforces that the event payload and extension protocol only ever grow relative to the checked-in baselines. The Rust API documentation describes the public Rust types; the protocol reference summarizes the active method surface.

docs.title: System Prompt Composition
docs.text: cookie agent keeps the system prompt deliberately small and inspectable. The Markdown body of the selected agent document is the base prompt. Parsing removes only trailing newlines and restores one final newline; frontmatter configures the agent but is not copied into prompt text.

docs.title: Composition order
docs.text:
For a root or delegated run, the engine composes the model request in this order:

  1. The selected agent document body becomes AgentSnapshot.composed_prompt.
  2. The session's runtime attachments are appended as a single <runtimes> block so the model knows which runtimes it can use and where relative paths resolve. The prompt and document fingerprints are updated.
  3. Trusted in-process tool providers may append bounded behavioral-policy sections. Sections retain provider provenance and update both prompt and document fingerprints.
  4. If skills are visible to the model, a generated available-skills listing is appended to that prompt. The prompt and document fingerprints are updated.
  5. agent_before_start plugins run in configured order. A plugin can replace the composed prompt or append an addendum, subject to the 128 KiB prompt limit. Each accepted change recomputes the prompt fingerprint.
  6. History assembly puts the final composed prompt in history[0] as the sole system turn.
  7. Root runs may then add a durable AGENTS.md context user turn. Loaded skill bodies follow as user turns, followed by normal session history.

Appended blocks are joined by a markdown horizontal rule ( --- ) so the boundaries between the authored body, the runtimes block, tool-provider sections, the skills listing, and a plugin addendum are visible. The authored body is first and carries no leading separator; a plugin replace_system_prompt replaces the whole prompt instead of appending to it.

The resulting agent snapshot is frozen in run_started. Model retries and fallbacks reuse that run policy and prompt fingerprint; configuration refreshes cannot alter an admitted run. Request assembly reuses the first event snapshot for the first attempt and refreshes session events only when a later attempt needs current history.

docs.title: Fingerprints
docs.text:
The document fingerprint covers the agent identity, strict frontmatter, and body. The prompt fingerprint covers prompt text only. The runtimes block, tool-provider sections, skill listings, and plugin composition update the effective fingerprints before run_started is persisted. Model-attempt events record the prompt fingerprint, and replay validation rejects attempt attribution that contradicts the frozen run snapshot.

AGENTS.md context is intentionally excluded from the system-prompt fingerprint. It has its own durable event, provenance, and user-role boundary.

docs.title: Tool-provider sections
docs.text:
Reviewed in-process providers can contribute cross-tool behavioral policy at run admission. Each section is normalized, validated, and rendered with an engine-derived identity:

<tool_instructions provider="builtin.delegate">
Available subagents:
- sub-fixer: Coder for anything that touches code
</tool_instructions>

Providers contribute in composition order: the base layer, then the global runtime, then the local coding runtime, each in registration order. Declaration order determines section order within a provider. Bodies are limited to 8 KiB per section, 16 KiB per provider, and 32 KiB across all providers. Any invalid content or overflow rejects run admission instead of truncating or omitting policy. The existing 128 KiB composed-prompt limit still applies.

This channel is for durable behavioral policy that must survive compaction and carry system priority. Per-tool guidance remains in typed tool descriptions; reference material belongs in explicit user-role context. Built-in providers should use compiled-in stable text. Local in-process provider and plugin code is reviewed and trusted like other installed code.

MCP providers are architecturally excluded. Remote MCP output remains delimited data and typed tool metadata; it cannot contribute durable system instructions, and no configuration switch enables that path.

docs.title: Runtimes block
docs.text:
The block lists every attachment of the session in attach order, with its kind, and for a coding runtime its canonical workspace and platform. Each entry also says whether, at admission, any of the runtime's tools is published under its attachment prefix because another runtime or the base layer offers the same name:

<runtimes>
<runtime name="global" kind="global" prefixed="false"/>
<runtime name="local_web" kind="coding" workspace="/home/me/web" platform="linux" prefixed="true"/>
<runtime name="labpc_api" kind="coding" workspace="/home/me/api" platform="linux" prefixed="true"/>
</runtimes>
File tools and bash of a coding runtime resolve relative paths against its workspace. Use workspace-relative paths for files inside it. When several runtimes offer a tool with one name, each is published as `<runtime name>_<tool>`; `prefixed="true"` marks a runtime whose tools carry that prefix.

Attribute values are XML-escaped. The block is frozen with the prompt: an attachment added or removed after admission changes the next run's block, not the current one.

docs.title: AGENTS.md context turn
docs.text:
At each root run start where AGENTS.md loading is on (the run agent's agent_md frontmatter, else [agent_md] enabled), each coding runtime the session is attached to discovers the applicable AGENTS.md files in its own workspace, and cookie agent stores their bounded content in one agent_md_loaded event per attachment that returned a file, naming the attachment. Files larger than 2 MiB are skipped and surfaced as AgentMdSkipped warning events. History replays the latest run's entries, the latest event per attachment, as one user turn, wrapped in a <system-reminder> block with each file delimited as:

<system-reminder>
As you answer the user's questions, you can use the following context:
# AGENTS.md
Codebase and user instructions are shown below. Be sure to adhere to these instructions.
IMPORTANT: These instructions OVERRIDE any default behavior and you MUST follow them exactly as written.

<contents from="/abs/path/AGENTS.md">
...
</contents>

IMPORTANT: this context may or may not be relevant to your tasks. You should not respond to this context unless it is highly relevant to your task.
</system-reminder>

With more than one attachment each <contents> element also carries a runtime="<attachment>" attribute. Events written before runtimes carry no attachment and count as the local runtime's.

Making this context a turn rather than system text keeps the stable system cache key independent of normal repository edits, preserves per-file provenance, and lets compaction pin the turn alongside loaded skill bodies. The rolling non-system cache breakpoint can still move when AGENTS.md context changes, which is the intended invalidation.

docs.title: Cache breakpoints
docs.text:
For capable Anthropic adaptors, cache strategy is structural rather than text injection. The engine clears prior markers, then can mark:

  • the non-empty system turn at history[0];
  • the final emitted tool definition; and
  • the last non-system history turn.

AGENTS.md context does not move or rewrite the system breakpoint. Tool schemas are separate request fields, so tool changes use the tool breakpoint instead of changing system text.

Anthropic also documents an automatic caching mode. Cookie agent intentionally uses the structural marker strategy above so system, tool, and rolling-history boundaries remain deterministic. OpenAI GPT-5.6+ likewise uses implicit or explicit cache breakpoints. Cookie agent's OpenAI system placement marks the last non-empty text part only when the first turn is an eligible system turn, while rolling considers only the latest user turn and marks its last non-empty text part. Either placement is omitted when that exact turn has no eligible text; Cookie agent does not search another turn. Assistant and tool-result content is never selected because those marker locations are rejected by the provider. Compaction resolves the same structural placements and shares the parent's cached prefix rather than using an isolated cache namespace. See the prompt-caching configuration reference.

docs.title: Agent matrix
docs.text:
Agent type System prompt Additional context Root Selected authored agent body, or the concise built-in default coding prompt; runtimes block, optional tool-provider sections, skill listing, and plugin composition Root-only AGENTS.md context turn, loaded skill bodies, then session history Delegated Frozen delegated agent body; runtimes block, optional tool-provider sections, skill listing, and plugin composition No filesystem AGENTS.md context load. Explicit inherited user/assistant text and ordinary child history remain separate turns. Internal Authored reserved internal agent body when available, otherwise its built-in prompt No AGENTS.md discovery, skill listing, or plugin prompt interception. Invocation-specific input is supplied separately.

The built-in approval, compaction, and title prompts are each roughly 100 bytes: one narrow instruction plus an output-format constraint. The synthesized default coding prompt is similarly concise. Authored internal agents can replace the built-in backend while retaining the same isolated invocation contract.

docs.title: Deliberate omissions
docs.text:
The system prompt does not contain an environment dump, tool-schema prose, MCP server instructions, filesystem inventories, or generic operational boilerplate. Tools and MCP capabilities are represented by typed request definitions and permission policy. Runtime state belongs in events or request fields. The narrow exceptions are the frozen runtimes block, which is needed to resolve relative paths and to tell runtimes apart, and the bounded set of authored behavioral-policy sections from trusted local providers: reviewed local code supplies them, fingerprints cover them, and the admitted run freezes them. The runtimes block is XML-escaped and skipped rather than truncated if the composed prompt is already at the byte limit. Changing, externally controlled, or redundant information remains in typed fields or explicit context turns.

See Agents, Events, and Configuration.

docs.title: Tool Reference
docs.text: Cookie Agent publishes tools according to the active agent's permissions and the capabilities of the selected model. Tool argument objects are strict: unknown fields and wrong types are rejected.

docs.title: Execution concurrency
docs.text:
Tool providers declare whether each tool is safe to overlap with sibling calls from the same model turn through ToolSpec::concurrency. ToolConcurrency is Exclusive by default; parallel execution requires an explicit Parallel declaration.

Tools Eligibility Coordination read, read_artifact, bash, webfetch Parallel Each call owns its execution and streaming state. write, edit Parallel Matching prepared serialization keys serialize mutations to the same target. delegate_subagent Parallel Delegate admission serializes durable child reservation and session creation internally. send_message Parallel Message acceptance serializes guard checks and the durable append inside the recipient actor. MCP tools Parallel Each MCP server's service mutex serializes calls to that server; different servers can overlap. skill, get_subagent_result, cancel_subagent Exclusive These calls interact with session-scoped state. Plugin and otherwise undeclared tools Exclusive External declarations cannot currently opt in.

All parallel-eligible calls in the turn are dispatched together without a fan-out limit. Exclusive calls run one at a time after the parallel calls have finished. Results remain associated with their tool call IDs, while terminal events are persisted in completion order.

docs.title: Tool call failures
docs.text:
A failed tool call terminates with a failure code and a message for the model:

Code Meaning execution_failed The tool ran, or tried to, and failed. operation_changed What the call was prepared and approved against changed before it ran, such as an MCP tool list or a restarted runtime. prepared_capability_lost The prepared call was lost, for example in a daemon restart between preparation and execution. permission_denied A permission rule denied the call. runtime_unavailable The runtime or MCP server that owns the tool is reconnecting or dropped during the call. The call is not retried for the model; the tool stays published while its owner reconnects. unsupported_platform The tool cannot run on this platform. invalid_url, redirect_error, timeout, transport_error, unsupported_content_type webfetch failures (see Webfetch).

docs.title: Webfetch
docs.text:
webfetch accepts {"url":"https://docs.quantumcookie.xyz/", "raw":false}. url is required; raw defaults to false. The URL must start with a lowercase http:// or https:// prefix; any other scheme is rejected with invalid_url before a request is sent. One permission check uses the initial URL including its query string. Without a matching rule the call is denied, and without any allow or ask rule for webfetch the tool is not advertised. Explicit ask rules still use the normal approval flow.

Output starts with four header lines (final_url, status_code, content_type, and truncated), followed by a blank line and the text body verbatim. Body newlines are physical newlines, not JSON escapes. Structured url, final_url, status_code, content_type, and truncated fields remain in result metadata. HTML (text/html or application/xhtml+xml) is rendered by html2text at width 80 unless raw is true. Text types, JSON, XML, JavaScript, form data, and +json/+xml types pass through as text; raw and non-HTML text use UTF-8 lossy decoding. Binary types are rejected, including in raw mode. Missing or invalid Content-Type is treated as application/octet-stream and rejected.

The request has a 30-second overall timeout, inherits environment proxies, and uses reqwest's default redirect policy (10 hops). Redirect hops are not permission-checked. HTTP error statuses are returned with their text bodies. There are no additional SSRF, host/IP, DNS, or userinfo checks.

Downloads are streamed to a fixed 16 MiB cap, or 4 MiB for HTML that is converted to text. Over-cap responses return the fetched prefix with truncated: true, not an error. The caps have no input or configuration parameter. Full results use the standard event log and result store. The standard Bounded policy retains oversized output and sends a preview to the model. read_artifact pages the retained header and body by physical line; its zero-based offset 5 starts at the body. Follow next_offset for successive pages. Metadata is separate and is not paged. read_artifact needs no permission rule.

Errors distinguish invalid_url, redirect_error, timeout, transport_error, and unsupported_content_type (which names the content type). permission_denied uses the standard policy-denial path and its structured tool_denied reason.

docs.title: Filesystem tools
docs.text:
read accepts filePath, plus optional zero-based offset and positive limit. The defaults return at most 2,000 lines or directory entries. The path is resolved when the call is prepared; the content is read when it executes. A text line longer than 4 KiB is cut and ends with a [line truncated: N more bytes] marker, and a page that would exceed the result size limit stops early with a continue with offset=N note (also reported as next_offset in the metadata). Media files are checked against the size limits before they are read in full.

write accepts filePath and complete content. edit accepts filePath, oldString, and newString, and requires the old text to identify one unambiguous replacement. Preparation checks the replacement against the current content so a mismatch fails before approval, but the edit itself is applied to the file's content at execution: changes made while an approval was pending are kept, and an oldString that no longer matches fails the call. Both tools publish through a staged file renamed over the target. Writes and edits that resolve to the same file share a serialization key and run one at a time, in call order, so same-file edits in one turn apply on top of each other.

Tool results may include image, PDF, audio, or video attachments. Attachments are validated, content-addressed, and supplied to models as file parts rather than embedded in text output.

docs.title: Media reads
docs.text:
When read targets an image (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP), PDF, audio file (MP3, WAV, Ogg, FLAC), or video container (MP4/MOV/WebM/MKV/AVI/FLV/MPEG/WMV/3GPP), the file is sniffed by content (never by extension alone), strictly validated, and retained as an attachment. Whether the attachment reaches the model depends on two checks, in order:

  1. Model capability. The selected model must declare the matching input modality in the catalog (for example image for image/png). If it does not, the call fails with a tool error naming the model and the missing capability.
  2. Family deliverability. The provider's wire API must accept the media kind either inside a tool result or in a following user turn (see the delivery matrix). If it does not, the call fails with a tool error naming the family.

Both rejections are ordinary tool errors: the model sees the reason and can recover (for example by asking the user, or by sampling the file through bash). Size is clamped to the smaller of the model's advertised limit and the provider's inline limit (Anthropic: 7.5 MiB raw images, 10 MiB once base64-encoded; Bedrock: 3.75 MiB images, 4.5 MiB documents, ≈18.7 MiB raw video; Vertex: 7 MiB images; Gemini API: 14 MiB for any media, keeping the base64 request under its 20 MiB cap; other families: 20 MiB images, PDFs, and audio, or 25 MiB video). Media goes in the tool result when the family's wire API accepts it there; otherwise, when the API accepts that kind in user messages, it is sent as a file in one emitted user turn immediately after the tool result. Each model also advertises per-kind count limits, enforced per request (catalog models: 20 images, 5 PDFs, 5 audio files, and 2 videos, 1 on Bedrock). When the history holds more parts of a kind than the limit, the oldest are replaced in the outgoing request by a placeholder such as [image omitted: over the model's per-request image limit]; the saved history keeps them. The elided count grows in steps of half the limit, so later media appends to an unchanged prompt prefix (and prompt cache) until the limit is reached again, at the cost of sending as few as half the limit's parts right after a step. The latest user message is never elided: a request fails only when that message alone attaches more parts than the limit. Media parts do not contribute to context fit estimates, except video, which carries a flat conservative cost.

MCP media blocks (images, audio, embedded resource blobs) follow the same gate and delivery selection. Blob resources without a declared MIME type are retained under the sniffed type. Results that would exceed the combined attachment budget keep what fits and degrade the rest to inline notes. The MCP wire format cannot author arbitrary additional messages.

Media does not survive context pressure. Tool-output elision removes the parent result and all of its emitted messages as one unit, and compaction checkpoints drop attachments. The model can re-read the source file to recover it.

docs.title: Media delivery
docs.text:
This matrix describes tool-origin media, not every input type the upstream API accepts. The effective model must also declare the modality and limits.

Effective adaptor family Images PDF Video Audio Anthropic Tool result Tool result No No Anthropic-compatible Tool result Tool result User turn on capable MiniMax models No Bedrock Converse Tool result Tool result Tool result on capable Nova models No OpenAI/compatible Responses, Azure Responses Tool result Tool result No No OpenAI Chat User turn User turn No No Azure Chat User turn No No No OpenAI-compatible Chat User turn User turn User turn on capable Kimi/Qwen models No Gemini, Vertex Gemini User turn User turn User turn User turn Cohere User turn No No No

docs.title: Bash
docs.text:
bash accepts a complete command, an optional timeout in milliseconds (default 120000; 0 never times out), interactive (default false), and background (default false). Interactive calls can receive bytes or EOF through the run.tool_stdin RPC while the call is active. Standard output and standard error are streamed separately during execution and retained as separate artifacts for the terminal result.

The command runs in its own session and process group (a job object on Windows). When the shell exits, whatever it left in that group is killed, so cmd & and nohup cmd & do not outlive the call; only a process that leaves the group, such as one started with setsid, does.

With background: true the call returns as soon as the command starts. Its result names the process ID, which is also the process group, so kill -- -PID stops the job early (taskkill //T //F //PID PID on Windows). The job keeps the same timeout and process-group cleanup. When it exits, the engine accepts one producer message owned by tool { tool_call_id } that steers into the active run or wakes the idle session: a <background_bash from="PID"> block with the command, the exit status and duration, and the job's standard output and standard error previewed exactly like a tool result: the first and last lines of each stream, with a read_artifact hint into the retained artifact for anything omitted. The job reports only after its starting call is committed as completed. It is killed without a report if that call is cancelled before it commits, if a revert removes the call, if its session is deleted, or when the daemon stops. background cannot be combined with interactive.

docs.title: Retained tool output
docs.text:
Tools declare ToolOutputDeclaration::Single or an ordered list of 1 to 8 named streams. Names are unique, case-sensitive ASCII path segments, 1 to 64 bytes, using letters, digits, _, -, and .; . and .. alone are forbidden. The same validator governs declarations and the stream argument of read_artifact.

The runtime keeps bounded previews and counts of accepted text chunks in memory. A stream that fits its preview is stored nowhere else: the result output holds all of it and it has no artifact. Once a stream outgrows its preview, its bytes are buffered and written in batches to a temporary file, hashed as they are written, and published as a full artifact at completion. An artifact keeps at most the first 128 MiB of a stream; past that only the last mebibyte is kept, after a marker line counting the dropped bytes, and the stream's dropped_bytes and the result's read hint report the loss. A single output has at most one artifact; named output gets a generic manifest when any stream has an artifact, and the manifest lists every declared stream. Declaration order determines model rendering. Bash uses the same named-output interface as other tools; it does not build its own retained-output manifest.

Each stream receives its own configured [tool_output] line/byte preview limits. Only truncated streams receive a read_artifact(artifact="<digest>", stream="<stream>", offset=...) hint, where the digest identifies the manifest. Single-output hints omit stream and the heading. A partial-line byte cut points back to that line, so readback does not skip unseen text. Aggregate preview construction also reserves 16 KiB for headings/hints inside the existing 2 MiB output bound; when necessary, previews are reduced with truthful read hints.

ToolProgress.output carries at most 8 typed chunks and 64 KiB of authoritative text per delta. Its optional display is independent UI text. The message and display fields are each limited to 1 KiB; the runtime caps their cumulative live-presentation budget at 64 KiB per call without stopping authoritative output. Final display replaces live display and has its own 64 KiB bound. Control characters are sanitized while newlines and tabs remain usable in display text. Display is never included in model history.

Executors return ToolCompletion: Single/Named supplies terminal output once, whereas Streamed finalizes accepted deltas without resending them. Resupplying terminal output after streaming is an error. Failures and cancellation preserve accepted output as incomplete, retain the correct terminal status, and expose the error alongside output previews to the model. Terminal events carry retained_output references and final display; replay does not recapture chunks.

The self-paginating read, read_artifact, and get_subagent_result tools declare an absolute truncation opt-out. Their requested page is returned in full without artifact retention or truncation metadata, regardless of [tool_output]. Callers bound these results with each tool's offset/limit arguments. A requested page above the event schema's 2 MiB output limit fails with a resource-limit tool error; it is never silently truncated. The delegate_subagent terminal result also opts out, because its teaser preview is bounded by [subagent_output] instead; the owner of the delegation flow is the only place it is bounded. MCP and plugin tools remain subject to normal truncation. External opt-out would require a future extension-protocol capability and is not currently authorable.

Artifacts are content-addressed by SHA-256, deduplicated, and newly created with mode 0600 on Unix. Their digest is verified when content is first read. A missing or corrupt artifact produces a normal tool error and does not prevent the engine or session from opening. Artifacts are written without fsync and without a store-wide lock (each publish is one atomic rename), so a crash or power loss can lose an artifact a durable event already references. Reads then report the output as unavailable, and model history replaces a lost attachment with a short note instead of failing.

Artifacts are collected only when a session is reverted. The revert deletes the digests that the cut-away events (and any delegated children the revert deletes) referenced, directly or through a generic manifest, unless an event still in the tree's logs references them too. The sweep is skipped while any session of the tree runs or a capture is still publishing its terminal references. Artifacts orphaned any other way, such as by a crash or a cancelled capture, stay in the tree's artifacts/ directory until the tree is deleted.

Artifact lookup uses the read_artifact tool:

Argument Meaning artifact The 64-character lowercase SHA-256 digest a hint names stream Optional declared stream name of a named-output manifest offset Optional zero-based line offset; default 0 limit Optional line count; default and maximum 2000

read_artifact is a base-layer tool. It needs no permission rule: it is always sent to the model and every call is allowed, whatever the agent's rules, because it can reach only artifacts stored in the calling session's own tree. A digest that names content another tree stored does not resolve. Digests are content-addressed SHA-256 references, not random secrets. Malformed digests (bare artifact:// URIs, the internal sha256/ form, uppercase or short digests) and invalid stream names are rejected. read reads only the filesystem.

Artifact reads return the stored content without unwrapping JSON. Normal single-output artifacts contain the original full text. Named-stream artifacts contain their complete individual text. Compaction retry artifacts may contain serialized tool-content JSON, including output text, metadata, and references to original truncation artifacts. Their markers identify this format and expose usable IDs without requiring durable elision events. Follow any nested truncation reference to retrieve the original full output rather than its serialized preview.

Without stream, read_artifact reads stored text as-is, including manifest JSON; it does not merge streams. stream selects a declared name from the generic manifest. This is content-based and works for results, diagnostics, or any other valid declared name, not just Bash streams. Unknown names and selection on non-manifests are errors. Stored ArtifactReference values keep the internal artifact://sha256/<digest> form, which is not a read_artifact argument.

Returned pages include next_offset metadata when more lines remain. A zero limit fails; larger limits are capped at 2000 lines. Pages over the 2 MiB terminal-result limit fail and must be requested with a smaller limit. Missing and corrupt artifacts produce tool errors.

{"artifact":"aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa","stream":"results","offset":0,"limit":200}

docs.title: Goal checklist tools
docs.text:
goal_get returns the current root goal's objective, status, revision, and entire checklist. goal_update { items } replaces the entire ordered checklist; each item contains only description and finished, with no item ID. The session actor serializes replacements, and the last accepted update wins. The tool has no goal_id or expected_revision parameter or lost-update protection. Its target is the current/latest session goal when the engine actor accepts the update, so an older run's update can intentionally affect a newly activated active or paused goal. Both tools are available only for root goals that are active or paused at run admission; lifecycle changes do not change an already-admitted run's tool set. Updates reject if the current goal is absent or terminal, even when the tool remains in an admitted run. Engine-owned goal IDs and revisions remain; SessionGoalLifecycleParams.goal_id and expected_revision apply to user lifecycle RPC controls, not model checklist updates.

The model cannot set an objective, pause, resume, or cancel. Empty checklists preserve the active or paused lifecycle; nonempty all-finished checklists complete it even while paused. The root must verify evidence before marking items finished. Both tools return the full state without display truncation. Their existing permission actions are read and write, respectively, both with resource goal:current. Ordinary permission matching, deny/ask rules, and the unmatched default still apply.

docs.title: Delegation and skills
docs.text:
Delegation tools start, inspect, and cancel owned subagent sessions. Skill tools load configured skill instructions for the current turn. Their availability and targets are derived from the frozen agent policy.

When delegation is available, its provider also freezes the currently eligible target IDs and agent descriptions into the run's system prompt under <tool_instructions provider="builtin.delegate">. The list uses the same depth ceiling and enabled-target filtering as delegate_subagent; no section is added when no target is available.

delegate_subagent, get_subagent_result, and cancel_subagent address subagents by a short tree-unique handle (<agent_type>_<8 hex>, e.g. explore_1a2b3c4d) or a full session UUID. A handle is generated when the session is created and resolves only within the caller's tree; a partial handle, another tree's handle, or a fabricated value is rejected with a self-repairing error that lists the live candidates as handle — description — status plus their UUIDs. Start and completion notices pre-wrap the handle, for example Subagent started. [subagent session explore_1a2b3c4d] and [subagent session explore_1a2b3c4d; completed; 79 lines; use get_subagent_result with session_id "explore_1a2b3c4d" for the full output]. The completion notice previews the report per [subagent_output], with its line breaks and tabs kept and other control characters folded to spaces. A report over the limit shows its first and last lines around a marker such as [… 200 lines omitted. Read more: get_subagent_result(session_id="explore_1a2b3c4d", offset=20)]; a complete one ends in full output shown. Terminal and lifecycle results keep the UUID under the unified session_id metadata key and add handle. resume_session_id accepts the same two forms, and a terminal child woken by send_message reports as running until its new turn ends.

docs.title: Agent messaging
docs.text:
send_message delivers a durable message to another session in the same delegation tree. It replaces the removed steer_subagent tool; see the migration notes. Its argument object is strict: to is the recipient handle or full session UUID, body is the markdown message text, and optional mode is steer (default) or queue. The recipient argument is named to; the earlier recipient_session_id spelling is not an alias and fails with send_message:invalid_arguments. A non-UUID recipient is resolved as a handle in the sender's tree; if it matches no live peer the send fails with the self-repairing unknown subagent reference error rather than a send_message: code.

Calls use the message permission action. The resource label is the recipient's relationship to the sender — parent, child, sibling, or * for any other same-tree peer — derived from stored session-origin metadata. Messaging is deny-by-default and the tool is hidden until an agent document or session overlay declares a message allow or ask rule. Denied calls use the standard policy-denial path and ask rules use the normal approval flow; there is no messaging-specific permission error.

A successful result means durably accepted: the message is persisted in the recipient's event log and survives a daemon restart. It does not mean the recipient has seen or consumed the message. The result carries message_id, the effective mode, and recipient_state (running, queued, or waking_finished). A steer send joins a running recipient's next safe model-request boundary; a queue send is claimed into the recipient's prompt at the next safe boundary. Idle and finished recipients are woken through the producer reconcile path, resuming the session with the message as input. There is no inbox tool.

Failures are explicit tool errors with stable codes:

Code Meaning send_message:disabled [messaging] enabled = false send_message:invalid_arguments Missing, unknown, or wrongly typed arguments, including the removed recipient_session_id spelling send_message:invalid_body Empty body or body over max_body_bytes send_message:unknown_session Well-formed recipient UUID that names no session send_message:not_tree_peer Well-formed recipient UUID in a different delegation tree send_message:self_send Sender targeted its own session send_message:inbox_full Recipient has max_pending_per_session pending agent messages; nothing was admitted send_message:max_hops_exceeded The message chain exceeded max_hops send_message:inflight_full The directed pair already has max_inflight_per_pair unacknowledged messages send_message:engine_shutdown The send raced daemon shutdown

Retries are safe: the idempotency key derives from the sender session, run, and tool call, so a retried call returns the original message_id and delivers once. Two loop-safety guards reject sends, and each can be disabled: max_hops <= 0 turns off hop counting (hop metadata is internal and never appears in the delivered envelope), and max_inflight_per_pair = 0 turns off the per-pair window. A pair message counts as unacknowledged while accepted, admitted, claimed, or released, and is acknowledged once consumed or discarded. See Agent Messaging for the settings and the agent messaging spec for the full contract.
